newsitem.title: JAPAN: Okinawans sceptical about U.S.-Japan bases deal.
newsitem.headline: Okinawans sceptical about U.S.-Japan bases deal.

text.p: Long-disgruntled residents of Okinawa appear less than thrilled by a U.S.-Japanese deal meant to end a row over the huge American military presence in the southern Japanese prefecture.

"There is strong opposition among municipalities which will be hosting those facilities in the future," Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota told a news conference after U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry and Japanese officials announced the agreement in Tokyo on Monday.
But Ota said he took note of the fact that the Tokyo central government had met some of his earlier requests.
"This means that the prefecture's demands for the first phase of the bases reduction programme would have been met."

A public outcry against U.S. bases flared up in September 1995 after the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen, since jailed. More than 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan are on tiny Okinawa, in the East China Sea about 1,000 km (650 miles) southwest of Tokyo.
Under Monday's agreement, the U.S. military will return one-fifth of the 58,000 acres (23,500 hectares) it takes up on Okinawa, but keep all the 28,000 troops it has on the island.
Officials from towns to which military facilities will be moved were especially angry at the agreement.
One of them is Nago, a possible site for a new floating helicopter base to replace the Futenma Air Station now located in Ginowan, southern Okinawa.
"The central government officials have ignored us locals again," a vexed Nago Mayor Tetsuya Higa told a news conference. "They still don't understand the feelings of Okinawans."

As soon as Monday's agreement was announced, Higa lodged a protest with the Ota's prefectural government and the U.S. consulate in Okinawa. "We will continue to protest, irrespective of what Tokyo thinks," Higa said.
"Moving things from right to left inside the same cage isn't going to change anything in Okinawa," said Mayor Masakata Togen of Ginowan city, which now hosts Futenma Air Station.

Other prominent critics included Professor Seiichi Sakugawa of Okinawa University, who spearheaded a movement to hold a provincial referendum in August which overwhelmingly approved a resolution seeking reduction of U.S. bases.

"The agreement is far from what Okinawans want," Sakugawa told a news conference. "If the stipulated land is actually returned, that would be one step forward. But I don't see how it can go smoothly, given the relocation conditions."
Ota, who has led the anti-bases movement, said it was now up to the central government to persuade reluctant local governments to host the facilities to be moved.
Ota had previously tried to force the closure of all U.S. bases in Okinawa but backed off after winning promises of central government help to boost the sagging Okinawa economy.
